deep.reconstruction:
Context: notebook page 78, following Hilbert's aphorisms on arithmetic and function theory. He builds an explicit continuous, strictly increasing bijection f of [0,1] onto [0,1] with f(Q) = Q, and shows f is not analytic.

(1) Construction. Write x in [0,1] in binary, x = 0.b1 b2 b3 ... Cut the digit string from the left into blocks from the complete prefix code {1, 00, 01}. Replace each block by one ternary digit: 1 -> 2, 00 -> 0, 01 -> 1. Read the result as a ternary fraction; that number is f(x).
- The code is a prefix code, so the parsing is unique.
- Its block lengths 1, 2, 2 satisfy 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 1, so the parsing never gets stuck.
- The map on digit strings preserves lexicographic order, because 00 < 01 < 1 matches 0 < 1 < 2.
- Geometrically: the dyadic interval coded by a block word of total binary length L with k blocks goes onto the triadic interval of length 3^{-k}. The images tile [0,1] in the same order.

Hilbert's worked example: x = 0.10100011101011011001... parses as
1|01|00|01|1|1|01|01|1|01|1|00|1
which gives 2 1 0 1 2 2 1 1 2 1 2 0 2, so f(x) = 0.2101221121202..._3, as on the page.

(2) Properties he claims.
- f is monotone and one-to-one, and its inverse is the reverse substitution.
- Rational arguments give rational values, and every rational value is attained at a rational argument. Justification (mine): a number is rational iff its expansion is eventually periodic. Parsing an eventually periodic binary string by a finite prefix code is a finite-state transduction, so it yields an eventually periodic ternary string. The same holds for the inverse substitution 2 -> 1, 0 -> 00, 1 -> 01.

(3) Continuity. The only problem points are numbers with two expansions, i.e. dyadic rationals w1000... = w0111... Hilbert checks that both expansions give the same ternary value:
- 0.1000..._2 = 0.0111..._2 gives 0.2000..._3 = 0.1222..._3 (parse 01|1|1|...).
- 0.11000..._2 = 0.10111..._2 gives 0.22000..._3 = 0.21222..._3.
- 0.01000..._2 = 0.00111..._2 gives 0.1000..._3 = 0.0222..._3 (parse 01|00|... versus 00|1|1|...).
Completing his argument (mine): case 1 covers the ambiguity occurring at a block boundary, and case 3 covers it occurring after a pending '0'. Case 2 is just case 1 after the prefix '1'. A monotone map whose image is all of [0,1] with no gaps is continuous.

(4) Non-analyticity. Take a dyadic point α = 0.ν1...νn 000... with f(α) = 0.ν̄1...ν̄N 000..._3. Set x' = α + 2^{-(n+2m)}, m > 0, i.e. append (2m-1) zeros and then a 1.
- The new digits parse into (00)^{m-1} followed by 01 (or similar), so f(x') = f(α) + a/3^{N+m} with a ∈ {1,2}.
- Hence the difference quotient is (f(x') - f(α))/(x' - α) = a·2^{n+2m}/3^{N+m} = a·(2^n/3^N)·(4/3)^m.
- This tends to ∞ as m -> ∞.
So at every dyadic rational, a dense set, f has no finite (right) derivative, and therefore f is not analytic.
errors: No real mathematical error. The continuity argument is sketched only by examples: case 2 is redundant, and the general reduction to cases 1 and 3 (ambiguity at a block boundary versus after a pending 0) is left implicit.
In the derivative step, a = 1 or 2 and the exact exponent depend on block alignment at position n. Hilbert's 'a = 1,2' gestures at this; the limit is (4/3)^m -> ∞ in any case.
Only one-sided difference quotients along a sequence are shown. This suffices to rule out a finite derivative.

Unremarked: f is in fact a singular function. Local slopes per block are 2/3 (block 1) and 4/3 (blocks 00, 01), and their geometric mean is sqrt(8/9) < 1, so f' = 0 almost everywhere. 'Not analytic' is a much weaker conclusion than what is true.

results.what: Explicit strictly increasing homeomorphism of [0,1] built by recoding binary digits through the prefix code {1,00,01} -> {2,0,1} and reading the result in base 3; it maps Q∩[0,1] onto Q∩[0,1].
results.modern_name: Digit-substitution (finite-automaton / transducer) homeomorphism; related to Minkowski's ?(x), Salem- and de Rham-type singular functions
results.usually_credited_to: Minkowski ?(x) (1904); Salem (1943) for explicit singular monotone functions; abstract existence of an order isomorphism Q->Q via Cantor (1895)

results.what: Continuity verified via the two binary expansions of dyadic rationals mapping to the two ternary expansions of one triadic rational.
results.modern_name: Well-definedness of digit maps at dual expansions

results.what: Difference quotient a·2^{n+2m}/3^{N+m} -> ∞ at every dyadic rational, so infinite derivative on a dense set and f is not analytic.
results.modern_name: Infinite derivative on a dense set / non-analyticity of a rational-preserving homeomorphism
results.usually_credited_to: context of Weierstrass/Stäckel questions on functions rational at rationals (Stäckel 1895)

deep.surprise_reason: A neat, explicit, digit-recoding homeomorphism with f(Q) = Q and infinite derivatives on a dense set. It anticipates the flavour of Minkowski's ?(x) and Salem-type singular functions, but the mathematics is elementary. Hilbert does not notice that it is singular (f' = 0 a.e.). It is a notable unpublished detail rather than a major result.

checkable.asserts: Truncations of Hilbert's example: x ≈ 0.10100011101011011001_2 maps to 0.2101221121202_3 (finite prefixes correspond block by block).
With n, N fixed positive, the difference quotient tends to oo (it equals (2**n/3**N)*(4/3)**m).
The mean log-slope is negative, so f' = 0 a.e. (f is singular); this is not stated by Hilbert.

transcription_corrections: The binary example is most likely x = 0,10100011101011011001... (20 digits) rather than 0,1010001110101101011001... (22 digits). Only the 20-digit string parses (1|01|00|01|1|1|01|01|1|01|1|00|1) to the page's 0,2101221121202; the 22-digit version gives 0,21012211211202.
'für jede [?] Stelle' is probably 'für jede solche Stelle' (or similar). The point is α = 0,ν1ν2...νn000..., and the next line should read f(α) = 0,ν̄1ν̄2...ν̄N 000...
In the x' line, 'x' = α + 1/2^{n+2m} (m > 0)' is correct. The note 'a = 1,2' belongs to f(x') = f(α) + a/3^{N+m}.
'umkehrbar eindeutige' = bijective; 'als Trialbruch gelesen' = read as a ternary fraction.
